title: SLO Adoption to Capacity Execution Handbook
author: Aisha Malik
body:
Summary
  -------
  This handbook operationalizes the path from an agreed SLO to concrete capacity actions and incident responses. It stitches together SLO definition, error budget policy, capacity provisioning, runbook responses, incident review expectations, and the operational tooling required to automate and measure each step. The goal is to give service owners and SREs a single canonical procedure for turning SLOs into repeatable, auditable capacity decisions.
  
  When to use this document
  ------------------------
  - New service onboarding where SLOs need to be translated to capacity runway.
  - Revalidating SLOs during major product changes or traffic-pattern shifts.
  - Triage when an error budget is burning faster than forecasted.
  - Post-incident corrective actions that require capacity changes.
  
  Definitions
  -----------
  - SLO (Service Level Objective): Target value for a measurable metric (e.g., p95 latency <= 250ms, availability >= 99.95%).
  - Error budget: 1 - SLO (e.g., 0.05% allowed downtime over a 30-day window).
  - Headroom: Spare capacity reserved to absorb unexpected demand without breaching SLO.
  - Capacity escrow: Pre-allocated, short-term capacity pool that can be unlocked when error budget depletion or surge is detected.
  
  Owners and responsibilities
  ---------------------------
  | Role             | Responsibility |
  |------------------|----------------|
  | Service Owner    | Define SLOs, own business tradeoffs, approve capacity commits. |
  | SRE Team         | Map SLOs to capacity, maintain runbooks, perform on-call actions. |
  | Platform Infra   | Provision reserved capacity, maintain autoscale policies & quota exports. |
  | Observability    | Maintain SLO telemetry, provide dashboards and alerting templates. |
  | Finance/Cost Ops | Approve long-term committed capacity and track cost impact. |
  
  SLO -> Capacity mapping (high level)
  ------------------------------------
  1) Validate SLO measurability
     - Ensure a production-grade signal exists (e.g., request latency, error codes, success rate) with 99.99% ingestion fidelity.
     - Define window for SLO evaluation (30d rolling is default; 7d for high-velocity changes is OK for experimentation).
  2) Define steady-state capacity based on baseline traffic profile
     - Use recent 90-day traffic histogram.
     - Generate per-quantile latency profile and tail behavior for each model/route.
  3) Compute required headroom to satisfy SLOs under expected variance
     - Run Monte Carlo or stress-simulations: simulate bursts, cold starts, and model eviction scenarios.
     - Convert predicted token/sec or qps into GPU allocation using benchmarked throughput curves.
  4) Establish capacity escrow policy
     - Reserve 10–25% short-term escrow for burst absorption; higher for multi-tenant or tail-sensitive workloads.
  5) Tie error budget thresholds to escalation and automation (see Error Budget Policy below)
  
  Concrete thresholds and examples
  --------------------------------
  - Example service: realtime-chat
    - SLOs: p95 latency <= 300ms, availability >= 99.95% (30d)
    - Baseline qps: 120 qps avg, 900 qps 95th
    - Headroom target: 35% (to account for distribution heavy tails & cold-models)
    - Escrow: 2 extra GPU instances (equivalent to +40% of steady-state) unlocked for 90 minutes per trigger
  
  Error Budget Policy (operationalized)
  -------------------------------------
  1) Error budget windows and thresholds
     - Green: >= 80% remaining — normal operations.
     - Yellow: 35%–80% remaining — notify Service Owner, increase sampling frequency of synthetic canaries to 1/min.
     - Red: < 35% remaining — auto-unlock capacity escrow for a single 90-minute burst; page SRE on-call and open a triage channel.
     - Exhausted: <= 0% — initiate emergency incident response, apply traffic shaping and soft-degradation per the degradation matrix.
  2) Automated actions tied to thresholds
     - On Yellow: increase synthetic canary rate; run traffic-mirroring to shadow infra to validate mitigation plans.
     - On Red: platform API call to unlock escrow; if platform is unavailable, run manual provisioning checklist (see Runbook steps).
     - On Exhaustion: enforce tenant-level throttles based on token-priority ledger; initiate canary rollback to previous model-version.
  
  Capacity escrow lifecycle
  -------------------------
  - Allocation: Platform Infra sets a short-term reservation under the service tenancy; documented in the reservation ticket with time-to-live (TTL).
  - Unlock path: Observability triggers unlock via orchestration API when error budget hits Red. Unlock must be auditable (incidents and tickets auto-created).
  - TTL and cooldown: Escrow grants last 90 minutes; if still needed, SRE must approve an extension via the capacity ticket board.
  - Reconciliation: Finance receives daily reports of escrow consumption and cost attribution.
  
  Runbook: rapid-response capacity unlock (condensed)
  --------------------------------------------------
  Trigger: Alert state = RED for error budget or p99 latency spike > 2x baseline for 10m.
  1) Acknowledge alert and post to #sre-triage channel with initial hypothesis + metrics snapshot (p50/p95/p99, qps, CPU/GPU utilization).
  2) Execute automated unlock: 
     - CLI: rwdctl capacity unlock --service realtime-chat --pool escrow-short --duration 90m --reason "error-budget-red"
     - If CLI fails, follow manual provisioning: open cloud console, add 2x GPU nodes to service pool, attach model runtime.
  3) Shift traffic: enable soft-priority lane (80/20 split) to favor low-latency critical routes.
  4) Monitor: validate p95 latency and availability every minute for 30 minutes. If metrics recover, start graceful drain of escrow.
  5) Post-incident: open capacity-reconciliation ticket and flag for incident review.
  
  Incident review standards for SLO-driven incidents
  -------------------------------------------------
  Required artifacts for any incident that touches SLOs or capacity:
  - Incident timeline with 1-min granularity for first hour, 5-min granularity thereafter.
  - Error budget burn chart and attribution by tenant/route/model.
  - Capacity action log: who unlocked escrow, CLI commands, timestamps.
  - Synthetic canary traces and representative request IDs.
  - Hypothesis table: suspected root causes and evidence for/against each hypothesis.
  
  Postmortem expectations
  - Classification: severity (sev-1..sev-4), SLO impact window, and whether error budget was consumed.
  - Action owners: each remediation must have an owner and ETA (max 30 days for critical fixes).
  - Capacity follow-up: schedule a capacity re-run (simulation) with adjusted headroom assumptions and publish results.
  
  Operational tooling and telemetry
  --------------------------------
  - Mandatory observability signals
    - request.latency.{p50,p95,p99}
    - request.success_rate
    - gpu.utilization.per-instance
    - token.throughput (tokens/sec)
    - synthetic.canary.latency and canary.success_rate
    - error_budget.remaining (30d rolling)
  - Alert rules (examples)
    - page_when: error_budget.remaining < 35% for 10m
    - warn_when: p95_latency > 1.5x SLO for 5m
    - auto-unlock: error_budget.remaining < 25% AND gpu.utilization > 85% for 5m
  - Dashboards to include
    - SLO scoreboard with rolling windows (7d/30d/90d)
    - Capacity heatmap: per-region, per-model, per-tenant
    - Escrow consumption panel with cost attribution
  
  Capacity simulation and validation
  ----------------------------------
  - Simulation inputs
    - traffic histograms (90-day), model sequence length distribution, quantization profile, cold-start rates
  - Outputs
    - recommended GPU count, headroom percentage, expected p95/p99 quantiles under bursts
  - Validation: run a shadow replay against isolated infra at 10–20% scale and verify SLOs hold under injected bursts.
  
  Degradation and fallback patterns (decision matrix)
  ---------------------------------------------------
  - Soft degrade: favor short responses, reduce beam/beam-like sampling, apply low-cost model variant.
  - Throttle: enforce token-level limits for noisy tenants; follow token-priority ledger.
  - Route-level fallback: route non-critical routes to lower-cost model or cached completions.
  - Full outage: switch to maintenance message and prioritize customer escalation flows per SLA.
  
  Communication and change control
  -------------------------------
  - Any change to SLO definitions, escrow sizes, or automated unlock rules requires:
    1) A documented proposal in the SLO change tracker.
    2) Review and approval by Service Owner + SRE lead + Finance if > $X/month additional cost.
    3) A canary rollout schedule and a rollback plan.
  - Weekly digest: SRE team publishes a weekly SLO-health email with top 3 burn drivers and budget forecast.
  
  Templates and checklists (appendix)
  ------------------------------------
  1) Incident evidence checklist (tick boxes)
     - [ ] Timeline (1m/5m)
     - [ ] Error budget chart
     - [ ] Capacity action log
     - [ ] Canary traces
     - [ ] Postmortem owner and 1st action
  2) Capacity repro request (fields)
     - Service, Region, Model, Baseline QPS, Desired headroom %, Escrow TTL
  
  Example YAML: autoscale policy snippet
  -------------------------------------
  apiVersion: rwd/v1
  kind: AutoscalePolicy
  metadata:
    service: realtime-chat
  spec:
    min_replicas: 4
    target_p95_latency_ms: 300
    headroom_percent: 35
    escalate_on_error_budget: true
    escrow_pool: escrow-short

  Related reading
  ---------------
  - SRE capacity playbooks, demand profiling guide, and synthetic-canary standards (see related_pages links above).
  - For platform CLI reference: docs.platform.internal/rwdctl
